summary: Defines the SNMPv2 management information base module for managing UDP implementations, so tools can read counters and listener information over SNMP. It was replaced by RFC 4113.

eli5.summary: It is a dashboard for UDP, the part of a computer that sends quick messages. A manager can look at how many were sent and received.

questions: how to monitor udp with snmp
what counters does the udp mib provide
subtitle: SNMP management objects for UDP implementations

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to monitor UDP usage across deployed systems, reading counters and checking which ports are listening, but there was no standard way to query this information.
tldr.mechanism: The UDP MIB defines a set of managed objects in SNMPv2 format that expose UDP statistics (datagrams sent, received, errors, undelivered) and a table listing active UDP listeners with their addresses and ports.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can poll SNMP agents to monitor UDP traffic, detect problems, and inventory listening services. RFC 4113 superseded it with IPv6 support.

today: RFC 2013 is an Internet Standard. It was superseded by RFC 4113, which added support for IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: What Is the UDP MIB
sections.content:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets network managers monitor and control devices. Managed objects—the things you can measure or control—are organized in a Management Information Base (MIB). A MIB module is a collection of related objects following a standard format written in SMI (Structure of Management Information).

The UDP MIB defines managed objects for monitoring UDP implementations. These objects expose counters for UDP traffic and a table of active UDP listeners. Originally defined in SNMPv1 (as part of MIB-II), this document defines the same objects in the newer SNMPv2 framework, which provides better semantics and conformance checking.
sections.eli5: It is a standard control panel on every computer with UDP. Managers can look at the dials and see what is happening.

sections.title: UDP Counters and Statistics
sections.content:
The UDP MIB defines four counter objects: udpInDatagrams counts all UDP datagrams delivered to applications on the local system. udpNoPorts counts datagrams received for which no application was listening at the destination port; these are typically discarded. udpInErrors counts datagrams that could not be delivered for reasons other than no listening port, such as checksum failures or length errors. udpOutDatagrams counts datagrams sent from the system.

Each counter is a 32-bit read-only value. These four objects give administrators visibility into the basic health and traffic patterns of UDP on a host: high inErrors suggests corruption or misconfiguration; high noPorts suggests probing or misrouted traffic; inDatagrams and outDatagrams track volume.
sections.eli5: Four dials show how many messages came in, how many had nowhere to go, how many were broken, and how many were sent out.

sections.title: UDP Listener Table
sections.content:
The UDP MIB includes a table, udpTable, listing every active UDP listener on the local system. Each row represents one listening port, identified by a local IP address and port number. The table contains two objects per row: udpLocalAddress (the IP address on which the port is listening) and udpLocalPort (the port number, 0 to 65535).

A special local address of 0.0.0.0 indicates a listener willing to accept datagrams on any IP interface of the node. Managers can query this table to discover which services are running on a host and on which addresses they are listening. The table rows are indexed by address and port, making it easy to check whether a specific service is active.
sections.eli5: A list of all the numbered mailboxes where this computer is ready to receive messages, and which network addresses they are connected to.

sections.title: Compliance and Object Groups
sections.content:
The UDP MIB specifies compliance statements and object groups for SNMPv2 conformance. All six objects (the four counters and two table columns) are grouped in the udpGroup. Systems implementing UDP management must implement all objects in this group to claim UDP MIB compliance.

The single compliance statement, udpMIBCompliance, declares that conforming SNMPv2 entities implementing UDP must support the udpGroup. This ensures that any system claiming to support UDP management via SNMP offers a consistent set of objects that applications can rely on.
sections.eli5: A rule that says if you claim to be a UDP management panel, you must have all six of these dials and buttons working.
